Sports.title: The $9bn pitch built for Ronaldo’s last World Cup – ‘Forever’ grass, artificial sunlight and closed roof
Sports.content:
Inside look at how FIFA transformed an NFL stadium into a World Cup pitch good enough for Cristiano Ronaldo and Virgil van Dijk, with grass flown across America and European lights.

The $9bn pitch built for Ronaldo’s last World Cup – ‘Forever’ grass, artificial sunlight and closed roof

It is only the best for Cristiano Ronaldo in what could be the final World Cup for the international football star.

Cold-climate grass will be flown in from Colorado and glowing 'grow' lights from the Netherlands will help produce a new pitch for Ronaldo, who will lead Portugal vs DR Congo on June 17 at Houston Stadium.



5 Cristiano Ronaldo could be playing in his final World Cup Credit: getty

Ronaldo will play under closed roof in World Cup

The 72,000-seat capacity venue will feature a closed roof and the inside temperature will be set to a perfect 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22.2 Celsius).

But the new 'forever' grass could be ripped out just days after the last 2026 FIFA World Cup match is played inside the normal home of the NFL's Houston Texans.

"We're building a grass pitch in that stadium as though it's been there forever and as though it's going to be there forever," Chris Canetti, president of the Houston World Cup Host Committee, exclusively told talkSPORT.



How the World Cup will make billion-dollar NFL stadiums good enough for Messi and Ronaldo

The fourth-largest city in America is scheduled to host seven World Cup matches inside NRG Stadium from June 14 through July 4, including two knockout contests.

Portugal, Germany, Netherlands, Sweden, Curacao, Congo DR, Uzbekistan, Cape Verde and Saudi Arabia are set to pursue the FIFA World Cup trophy inside a multi-purpose venue that sits next to the vacant Astrodome, cost $325 million to build in 2002 and could require a $1.4 billion renovation.



"It's a great stadium. There wasn't too much work that needed to be done," said Canetti, who previously served as the president of MLS' Houston Dynamo.

Except for a couple critical to-do list items at the core of a World Cup that could bring in $9 billion in revenue but has been shadowed by overpriced tickets and travel issues, including an award-winning referee being barred from attendance.



While NFL players campaign for grass fields in all 32 NFL stadiums, FIFA required the installation of the player-friendly surface in its American World Cup venues that will include Gillette Stadium (New England Patriots), Lumen Field (Seattle Seahawks) and SoFi Stadium (Los Angeles Rams and Chargers).

New pitch widened by removing seats

"In the previous editions of the World Cup, whether it's in Qatar or Russia or Brazil or South Africa, a lot of the stadiums were built from scratch," Canetti said.

"When the stadiums are built from scratch, they're built right to the FIFA spec book, right, so they are compliant with FIFA from day one.

How World Cup pitch is created in NFL stadium Cold-climate grass from Colorado

Growing glow lights from Netherlands to replicate sunlight

Sub-air ventilation

Irrigation system

22-inch sand base

Sod grown and rooted before first match (Germany vs Curacao on June 14)

Roof closed for World Cup matches in Houston

Temperature inside stadium set to 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22.2 Celsius)

Seats removed to widen the pitch area and make field FIFA compliant

5 New grass is being grown on the field with glow lights Credit: getty



5 World Cup signs have taken over NRG Stadium, the home of the NFL's Houston Texans Credit: getty

"We haven't built any stadiums here in the United States, Mexico or Canada. In particularly in the United States, we're using NFL-built stadiums, so they don't meet the FIFA spec book. They're great, awesome spectacles of venues. But the work needs to be done to bring them up to FIFA code.

"We had to make a major renovation this past summer where we took out some seats to widen the pitch area to make sure that there was enough pitch width for FIFA. If you were to go over to the stadium right now, you would see us installing the grass pitch."

NRG Stadium is built upon a concrete floor, which allows it to bounce between everything from the NFL to an all-encompassing annual rodeo.



"The surface is brought in for whatever the event is," Canetti said.

Artificial lights and 'comfortable' temperature

"If it's an NFL game, they're bringing in the artificial turf. If it's an NCAA basketball game, they're bringing in a hardwood floor. If it's Disney on Ice, they're bringing in ice. And if it's the rodeo, they're bringing in dirt."

To build a temporary NFL-turned-World Cup pitch good enough for Ronaldo, Virgil van Dijk and some of the best football players on the planet, sub-air ventilation and an irrigation system will be employed.

NRG Stadium's roof will also keep out the scorching Texas summer heat, while the inside temperature will be set to "very comfortable."

"There's a 22-inch sand base," Canetti said.

"The sod will go on. It'll be grown and rooted well before the first game.



"The roof will stay closed because it's a cold climate grass that's actually coming in from Colorado, and we will use these grow lights to artificially produce sunlight. The grow lights have come from the Netherlands, so a lot of technology and science goes behind this."

Ronaldo can silence critics in Houston

For the 41-year-old Ronaldo, there's also hope.

The Al-Nassr star also serves as Portugal's captain and is battling rival Lionel Messi for football's GOAT title.

5 Ronaldo is still very much the heartbeat of the Portugal squad Credit: getty

5 Ronaldo has won the European Championship and Nations League - all that's missing is the World Cup Credit: Getty



While critics insist that his country is better with Ronaldo off the pitch, a 'forever' field in Houston could help lead the fifth-ranked team in the world to the World Cup final.

"If a fan were to come into that stadium and not know any better -- or even a player, hopefully -- it'll look like that grass pitch has been there for the entirety of the stadium's life and as though it's going to stay there forever," Canetti said.

"Even though probably two days after the event is over, we unfortunately have to tear it out."

Sports.title: Tottenham confirm SECOND free signing of the summer as squad overhaul under Roberto De Zerbi continues after nightmare season
Sports.content:
Tottenham confirm SECOND free signing of the summer as squad overhaul under Roberto De Zerbi continues after nightmare season

Which England star has 7 GCSEs? Who has lost half of his finger? Test your knowledge of Thomas Tuchel's squad with our exclusive quiz HERE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Tottenham have announced their second free transfer of the summer in the arrival of Marcos Senesi.

Centre back Senesi, 29, left Bournemouth after four years at the end of last season upon the expiry of his contract, and waved an emotional goodbye to the Cherries fan base alongside Andoni Iraola.

He has now swapped red and black for white, and joins former Liverpool defender Andy Robertson in moving to north London on a free deal.

'It's a very special feeling to be a Tottenham Hotspur player,' Senesi told the club website.

'From the first moment, the Club has shown why they want me and how much they want me to be a part of what they are building. It's exciting and something I can't wait to be involved in.

'Every time I step on the pitch, I will do my best to make the fans proud and to take the Club back to the place it belongs. I want to win things with Tottenham and will do everything I can to make that happen.'

Tottenham have announced the signing of Marcos Senesi on a free transfer from Bournemouth

Manager Roberto De Zerbi, who led Spurs to safety last season, said: 'Marcos' experience, quality on the ball, and competitive edge will strengthen us defensively, as well as giving us flexibility in formation.

'He's comfortable playing in a possession-based team, reads the game very well and has the personality to thrive in a demanding environment.

'I also love his mentality and desire to keep improving and I'm looking forward to working with him and seeing the big contribution he can make to the team.'

Senesi's Bournemouth exit will potentially take him away from partner Kelci-Rose Bowers, who played for Bournemouth's Women's team.

They have become known as the club's 'power couple' and reportedly began dating in 2025, with the pair having since shared several snaps together on social media.

Kelci-Rose is a defender for the Cherries after beginning her youth career at Southampton, and outside of football she is a model.

Together, they have appeared to take several romantic holidays, and Bowers has 195,000 followers on Instagram. Bournemouth have, though, confirmed she is now too leaving the club.

Spurs are looking to sign another centre back in Jan Paul van Hecke, but have had an opening offer rejected.

The move could split Senesi from girlfriend, Kelci-Rose Bowers, who played for Bournemouth's women's team

Brighton value the 25-year-old Netherlands international at close to £70million but he only has one year left on his contract.

Chelsea also hold an interest but Van Hecke is well-known to Roberto de Zerbi after he played under the Tottenham coach during his time in charge of Brighton.

That dynamic will attract the defender to the move but Spurs need to get closer to Brighton's valuation.

There is an expectation that Cristian Romero will leave this summer and the club are clearly targeting reinforcements at centre back.

Earlier on Wednesday, though, it was announced Ben Davies had signed a new 12-month deal at Tottenham to extend his stay at the club into a 13th season.

Wales captain Davies only made five appearances during an injury-ravaged last season, but was praised by De Zerbi for his leadership during a tense and ultimately successful relegation battle in the Premier League.

Davies, who has appeared 363 times for Tottenham, was present for matches at Aston Villa and Chelsea before he helped with the team’s preparations before a final-day win at home to Everton.

However, Yves Bissouma will leave the club this summer when his contract expires on June 30.

Sports.title: 'Roy Keane pinned me to the wall as we travelled to Saipan'... As the World Cup kicks off without the Boys in Green, PHILIP QUINN - who was there - tells the inside story of Ireland's infamous 2002 pre-tournament bust up
Sports.content:
'Roy Keane pinned me to the wall as we travelled to Saipan'... As the World Cup kicks off without the Boys in Green, PHILIP QUINN - who was there - tells the inside story of Ireland's infamous 2002 pre-tournament bust up

Although Roy Keane was out of sight under the swaying palm trees, his accent, Corkonian and confrontational, was unmistakable.

'Take his bloody head off,' he barked from the shadows.

It was a humid night in May 2002 in the middle of the Pacific and the Republic of Ireland players, coaching staff, together with a handful of journalists, were enjoying a beachside bonding barbecue after an aching 22-hour trip from Dublin.

The 'we're all in this together' approach under manager Mick McCarthy extended to the journalists on the Irish football beat who had reported on the road to the World Cup.

We flew out of Tehran at midnight with our ticket punched to the finals in Japan and South Korea.

I recall the pilot announcing we had entered Iraqi airspace and he was permitting alcohol to be served. The roar at 29,000 feet carried half-way to Dublin - it had been an arid four days in Iran.

We were back on world football's greatest stage - something that briefly beckoned for the current team under Heimir Hallgrimsson this summer after their thrilling gate-crashing feats into the playoffs - and everyone was happy, from Bertie to Zig and Zag.

Well, not everyone. Roy Maurice Keane, for one.

Roy Keane shows his frustration during training in Saipan in May 2002

As we set out for the Far East, Ireland's leading player, the inspirational team captain, had the hump. He was antagonistic towards McCarthy, the FAI blazers and sections of the press, one of whom was me.

After fighting a winning battle with alcohol, Keane's road to recovery may have contributed to the seismic events of Saipan.

The simmering shifts in the plates under Keane were evident before we touched down in the middle of the world's deepest waters.

At Dublin Airport, Keano stayed sitting while the Taoiseach Bertie Ahern, a Manchester United lifer, offered his hand and posed for a snap.

When we stopped off at Amsterdam, he made a beeline for me in the departure lounge, clearly angered at reports of his no-show at Niall Quinn's Testimonial, the week before.

In fairness, he had a point as McCarthy had given him permission to skip the game. The better news line was to suggest Keane was a possible injury scare before the World Cup, which he was, with a knee that needed minding.

Keane felt slighted by the coverage and let me know what he thought of it. In Amsterdam, he pinned me to a wall and let rip. But for the arrival of Steve Staunton, I might have been the first casualty of the World Cup.

On the flight to Tokyo, Keane spoke briefly to journalists and stressed his displeasure at how his Sunderland absence was portrayed. His point was that he was on the 'plane and ready to play'.

For the barbecue gathering, the night after we touched down in Saipan, Keane's mood was not improved by the chronic state of the training pitch, which had one set of goalposts, and more than one pothole.

Keane and teammate Ian Harte in Saipan with manager Mick McCarthy

The skips containing the gear arrived late and the players initially had to train in the tops and shorts they brought with them, of which they had plenty. Also contrary to some suggestions, they also had footballs, if not the ones that FIFA would use in the finals, as they were delayed.

Even so, it was all a bit amateurish, which got under Keane's skin even if Saipan was intended to be about light training and getting accustomed to the humidity, while generating a team spirit to take into World Cup battle.

Which explained the barbecue. From memory, the spread was lavish, but it was the entertainment that turned heads - and nearly cost me mine.

A group of native Mariana Islanders, daubed in war paint, brandished burning spears which they threw at a board akin to an archer's target.

When volunteers were asked to stand in the line of fire, the local beer got the better of me and I went on to the raised stage.

It was then that Keano's cry carried across the sands - I knew then there would be no one-on-one exclusive interview that week with Ireland's captain.

Others that night were already plotting in that regard, and their diligence would be rewarded with interviews which blew the lid off Ireland's preparations for the finals and continues to provoke debate today.

That barbecue gathering spilled over into a local bar, The Beefeater, where players and press mingled until the wee hours.

Keane gave it a miss as socialising in a pub environment wasn't his thing at the time. In his younger days with Ireland, he would have been the last man standing on a night out.

It was probably just as well that Keane missed the moment where one Irish player, in all seriousness, asked aloud, 'Has anyone got a problem with my lifestyle?' He had a bottle of beer in each hand and a cigarette behind his ear at the time.

As for Keane, it seemed he had issues with just about everything and everyone on the island.

Mail soccer writer Philip Quinn

He fell out with Packie Bonner as he felt the goalkeepers hadn't put in a proper shift in training. That they started earlier than the outfield players, which is still the case, didn't cut it with Keane.

Returning to the hotel after that second day's training session, he informed McCarthy he wanted out of the World Cup and was going home.

Startled, McCarthy asked Keane was the problem the pitch, the gear arriving late, or was it him, the manager? Keane said, 'No. It's me.'

It took the intervention of Manchester United manager, Alex Ferguson, among others, in a series of overnight phone calls, to persuade Keane to change his mind, which he did in the nick of time to be registered with FIFA for the finals - Colin Healy had been put on stand-by by McCarthy.

Only the sense of calm, as we all found out, would be temporary.

Saipan was no stranger to volatility. Five miles across the shark-infested Saipan Bay lay the island of Tinian, from where the plane carrying the first atomic bomb, destined for Hiroshima, took off in 1945. The long runway was visible across the sound.

In World War Two, fighting between American and Japanese troops in Saipan in the summer of 1944 was as fierce as any in the Pacific theatre.

Forced back, inch by inch, to the highest point of the island, Japanese soldiers, and civilians too, threw themselves to death rather than give themselves up to the Americans. No surrender was also Keane's approach. Together with a group of press colleagues, I visited the 'Suicide Cliffs' during the week and paused for a moment's sombre reflection at the jagged rocks down below.

As an uneasy peace settled on the Irish party, McCarthy teed off with most of the squad, and the press corps, for a midweek round of golf.

A non-golfer, Keane stayed back in the hotel. With nothing to do, he agreed to four interviews, two to RTÉ, and one each to The Irish Times and the Sunday Independent.

The grenades he unpinned included his impending international retirement, strident criticism of the FAI and, to a lesser degree, McCarthy's management.

Roy Keane takes his dog Triggs for a walk after returning to his home in England

It was only a matter of time before the cat was out of the bag, to use a phrase of subsequent Irish manager, Giovanni Trappatoni, which led to Ireland competing in the World Cup without their best player. Keane's number six jersey was never used.

On reflection, there were mistakes on all sides. I felt then, and still do, that McCarthy was wrong to drag Keane to the Pacific retreat. Beer, barbecues and birdies were not Keane's thing.

Leaving Keane at home, to bring Triggs for walkies, before joining up with the party in the Japanese base of Izumo, was a safer option. Instead, McCarthy's 'one for all and all for one' approach, while admirable, backfired.

McCarthy also erred in calling the infamous team meeting after reading a transcript of Keane's explosive interview in The Irish Times and demanding if anyone had a problem to speak up. Keane was never going to ignore that challenge and as exchanges became heated between the two men, he let rip with a volley of vitriol which gave McCarthy no choice but to sanction the exit of his one world-class player.

I can still recall Paul Kimmage rapping on doors with a message that we were to hightail it into the team hotel next door for an emergency press conference.

When I asked Paul what the urgency was, he said, 'He's going home.' 'Who is,' I asked. 'Keane,' he replied. I don't think I ever moved as fast on the football beat.

That led to another image I'll never forget, that of McCarthy, sitting on a raised stage in a small conference room, informing the small band of journalists who had travelled to the island expecting to file little news, that he had decided to send Keane home.

Alan Kelly, Niall Quinn, Mick McCarthy, Milo Corcoran and Steve Staunton face the press

Doing his best to appear calm yet clearly strained by the enormity of what he felt compelled to do, McCarthy was flanked by Alan Kelly and Niall Quinn to his right, with Milo Corcoran, the FAI vice-president, and Steve Staunton, to his left.

The presence of three senior players was significant. They all endorsed McCarthy's call to banish Keane, a call which continues to shadow McCarthy to this day. It will never leave him.

In fairness to McCarthy, it would have required the skills of a diplomat and psychologist to stay onside with Keane, so tricky was the captain to handle at that time.

Had he spoken to Keane privately behind closed doors about the points raised in his newspaper interview, the outcome could have been so much different. Keane's gripes in print were nothing compared to his explosive tirade in public against his manager.

Even so, Keane must shoulder responsibility for the disruption to Ireland's World Cup plans. In prickly mood before leaving Dublin, he was picking rows left, right and centre before dropping the bombshell early on in Saipan that he was going home, only to then change his mind.

He was minutes away from missing the FIFA deadline for squads to be submitted when he relayed a message to McCarthy he would be staying.

By the time of the notorious team meeting two days later, his mood was anything but conciliatory.

When forced into a corner, prompted by a suggestion from McCarthy that he may have feigned injury to miss an Ireland game, he exploded. He called McCarthy 'a w****r; who 'could shove the World Cup up his a**e'.

Thereafter, the only route back into the tent was to withdraw his comments, only retreating was not in Keane's psyche, just as it wasn't for the Japanese soldiers on the island over half a century earlier.

Keane during the famous 1-0 victory over the Netherlands in Lansdowne Road in September 2001

Undoubtedly, Keane allowed his personal animosity towards McCarthy, whom he fell out with on his first Irish tour to the United States in 1992, to mask his responsibilities to his team-mates and to his country.

While leading by example on the pitch, he was publicly insubordinate to his manager off it and McCarthy felt compelled to draw a line in the sand and move on without his best player. Would Keane, had he been manager, acted any differently? I doubt it.

Yet, more than anyone, Keane had dragged the team unbeaten through the qualifiers. More than anyone, he had earned the right to perform in the greatest theatre of all.

He was 30 years of age and the keystone of the most successful Manchester United team of all time. His loss was immeasurable.

As for the FAI, they took their eye badly off the ball. Their delegation in Saipan was lightweight and this lack of leadership on the island was cruelly exposed. The late Corcoran, a mild-mannered sort, was never going to front up to McCarthy or Keane It meant there was no one on the island senior enough to prevent McCarthy from calling the infamous meeting or, when it was over, dragging McCarthy and Keane into a room to find a resolution.

Keane and McCarthy shake hands at the end of the Netherlands victory

Once the squad left Saipan, there was no way back for Keane, for all the handwringing of those desperate to broker a deal. Everyone did their bit, especially back home, no one more so than the late Tommie Gorman, who knew his football, on RTÉ.

Had Keane led Ireland into battle, who knows how the course of Irish football history may have been shaped? The teams in the 2002 World Cup lacked stellar quality, Brazil and Germany apart, and Ireland could have gone deep in the competition.

This was a squad, remember, with five subsequent Irish centurions, Staunton, Kevin Kilbane, Shay Given, Damien Duff and Robbie Keane, and with seven others who captained teams in the Premier League.

Duff won two Premier League titles, Steve Finnan won everything at Liverpool, including the Champions League. Ian Harte and Gary Kelly helped Leeds to the Champions League semi-finals.

This was a squad of quality, comparable to those at the finals of 1990 and 1994 under Jack Charlton.

With Keano, at his playing peak, wearing the number six jersey in the trenches, there was sufficient quality for Ireland to give anyone a bloody nose.

Pointedly, even without Keane, the team finished stronger than their opponents in all four games, which indicated that the heat and humidity of Saipan, after all, had been beneficial.

The entire Irish party was in Saipan for just six days. Six days that led to the nation holding its breath, just as they did in the penalty shoot-out in the 1990 World Cup.

Say it ain't so, Roy, they pleaded? Only, it was.

Sports.title: I've spent hours with Ben Stokes, ghostwriting his books and, yes, he's stubborn but he's also dedicated to England and determined to make up for Ashes nightmare. To jettison this icon over a curfew breach would be madness, writes RICHARD GIBSON
Sports.content:
I've spent hours with Ben Stokes, ghostwriting his books and, yes, he's stubborn but he's also dedicated to England and determined to make up for Ashes nightmare. To jettison this icon over a curfew breach would be madness, writes RICHARD GIBSON

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

This would be no way to end an England captaincy or international playing career. It would leave a blot on what will be a stellar sporting legacy.

Yes, Ben Stokes should be punished for breaking a team curfew that he himself was party to setting after last winter’s Ashes shenanigans, with a suspension for the remainder of the Test series with New Zealand. Throw in a hefty fine and final warning, too.

That is the kind of punishment truly commensurate with the crime of being alongside team-mate Gus Atkinson at the Rex Rooms nightclub in Chelsea in the early hours of Monday morning, where a member of the England team’s security staff was allegedly struck by Saracens rugby player Totoa Auvaa.

Anything more would be Draconian. The problem for the ECB as they mull over their options is the landscape against which this flouting of the team’s Cinderella time occurred.

Forced into taking action following months of boozy indiscipline in New Zealand and Australia from October to January, they came up with a midnight cut-off for players to return to their hotels while representing their country on overseas tours.

The ECB confirmed it would remain in place this summer, but its application has been questioned by many privately. One decorated ex-England international messaged me after the news broke on Monday, simply saying: ‘I just hate that curfew.’ A seasoned former county cricketer asked for clarification: ‘It doesn’t apply once a match is over, though, right?’

This would be no way for Ben Stokes' England career to come to an end. It would leave a blot on what will be a stellar sporting legacy

Stokes celebrates hitting the winning runs in the third Ashes Test at Headingley in 2019 in his most iconic innings

After all, it was not before or during a match, but after a victory. Few would have batted an eyelid had England’s drinking culture come to light during a winning rather than losing Test series against Australia. Post-match beers would have been viewed as a badge of honour.

Test cricketers are famous for sharing beers and reminiscing in the dressing room post match - drinking out of their Baggy Green caps is a rite of passage for Australia's players. Stokes himself made a point of referencing how much he was looking forward to joining his team-mates for a beer during the post-match press conference of England’s 115-run success at Lord’s.

Stokes could not hide his relief about getting back on track on the field after an Ashes tour he genuinely believed could have been historical but which went so wrong. He knew the performance would be scrutinised and in New Zealand, high-level opposition lay in wait.

Having a drink or two was a vehicle for releasing some tension. With 10 days between the first and second Tests, it was hardly an issue if two became four, or half a dozen. If you’re going to have a blow-out, this was the time.

There will be those that say this England team have a problem with alcohol, yet the truth is that they get so few chances to socialise that they are guiltier of going to excess than your average frequenter of pubs when they do.

It should be noted that Stokes, 35, has often given up booze completely, as was the case over the past few months when recovering from a fractured cheek socket. Such was his desperation to get back on the field and atone for defeat to Australia.

I have witnessed his dedication to getting back to playing for his country first-hand as ghostwriter of two books, including his autobiography Firestarter. During one knee injury, two-hour interviews would be carried out at his house with his leg raised in an ice compression machine.

It might sound incongruous but of all the cricketers that I have worked with on such projects, none have been more professional than Stokes.

His time management and commitment were always exemplary. On the rare occasions he could not make a meeting, or was going to be late, notification came well in advance. Once invested in a project, he is all in. We watched back his 135 not out in Leeds twice over, in his sports room, to recapture every thought that had entered his mind in securing that sensational success.

Stokes was relieved to get England back on track at Lord's after an Ashes tour he genuinely believed could have been historical but which went so wrong

Former England captain Michael Vaughan said this week that Stokes ‘was aggressive with people a couple of times after interviews' in Australia

Stokes would always do extra rehabilitation exercises to get back for England. Give him an eight-week recovery period and he will aim to do it in six. This is a man who wears his heart on his sleeve, almost literally. He loves playing for England and his Test number 658 and shirt number 55 adorn his left arm, part of a tapestry of ink that pays homage to his career.

Some might argue that he has wanted it too much, recently. Indeed, writing in The Daily Telegraph, Michael Vaughan said he had been sharing concerns about Stokes in the build-up to Lord’s.

He wrote: ‘In Australia, he was aggressive with people a couple of times after interviews. I have heard that he has not been shaking the hands of well-respected people in the game. It was odd at Lord’s that he did not come down to have his photograph taken with all the other England ex-captains as part of the 150th Lord’s Test celebrations. I thought that was a bad look. He does not seem to respect the past or other people doing their jobs.’

There is no doubt he is a singular man. One who is increasingly intent on doing things his way. It led to him clumsily using the phrase 'has-beens' about those who criticised England’s limited preparation for the Ashes last November.

Indeed, on Sunday when England coach Brendon McCullum was discussing Stokes’ willingness to listen to others about his batting in the wake of a recent decline, he said: ‘He only trusts a certain amount of people, which is no bad thing in life.’

One of them, his manager Neil Fairbrother has been navigating a way forward over the past 72 hours, just as he did in the days after the Bristol fracas in September 2017 that led to Stokes being found not guilty of affray.

It has been for talismanic performances, such as the iconic unbeaten hundred to beat Australia by one-wicket at Headingley in 2019, and four years of inspirational leadership and tactical nous that he has been remembered for since.

Very few can be compared to him as England’s Test captain: a 56 per cent win ratio is only marginally inferior to that of Mike Brearley, who led in 12 matches fewer.

As ghostwriter of his book, I've seen first hand his dedication to playing for England in the way he has done his rehab

Like Virat Kohli, Stokes has also been a champion of Test cricket, and the game cannot afford to prematurely lose any of those

Some of those who shelled out thousands of pounds to head Down Under last winter were left concerned by the image of the team, but the majority were more hung up on its aptitude.

Money will inevitably have some part to play for the ECB. Stokes is on a central contract worth seven figures annually which still has 16 months to run.

Like Virat Kohli, he has also been a champion of Test cricket, and the game cannot afford to prematurely lose any of those.

Hopefully, putting time between the incident and its final analysis will conclude Stokes’ actions were a mistake - but not one that should terminate the career of one of England’s greatest cricketers.

Sports.title: 'With Declan Rice, because of his physique and ability, maybe he could do a little bit more.' STUART PEARCE on 'streetwise' England's World Cup bid, how they can take the final step and what he learnt during a drugs test at 'magical' Italia '90
Sports.content:
Think of England at the World Cup and what do you see?

For some, the tape will roll all the way back to 1966 – Bobby Moore lifting the Jules Rimet Trophy, or Geoff Hurst hammering in the fourth, with Kenneth Wolstenholme’s commentary providing the soundtrack.

More recently, the mind turns to Jordan Pickford’s penalty save from Carlos Bacca against Colombia eight years ago, or Harry Kane’s miss from the spot against France in Qatar. A little further back, David Beckham’s red card and Michael Owen’s goal against Argentina.

At least as clear, though, are the snapshots from the Stadio Delle Alpi, in July 1990 - the closest England have come to reaching a World Cup final since beating West Germany at Wembley 60 years ago. That night in Turin, a heroic performance from Sir Bobby Robson’s team against West Germany ended in defeat on penalties, with the tears of Paul Gascoigne and Stuart Pearce that followed.

Pearce’s outstanding career is not defined by the spot-kick he drilled against the shins of Bodo Illgner, especially as he exorcised those ghosts by scoring twice in shoot-outs at Euro 96.

Because Pearce, now 64, played such a key role in England’s best World Cup team since 1966, he is ideally-placed to assess Thomas Tuchel’s side’s chances over the coming six weeks. As well as winning 78 caps, Pearce also coached the England Under-21 side from 2007-13, working as Fabio Capello’s assistant with the senior side in four of those.

Stuart Pearce, pictured at Grays Athletic Football Club, won 78 England caps, coached the Under-21 side from 2007-13 and worked as Fabio Capello’s assistant with the senior side

Pearce sees his penalty saved by Germany goalkeeper Bodo Illgner in the 1990 World Cup semi-final

Over coffee in the club house at Isthmian League club Grays Athletic, Pearce argues that England’s willingness to embrace football’s dark arts have helped them become a more competitive side. The results bear that out, with two finals, a semi-final and a quarter-final in major tournaments since 2018.

‘We certainly are a cuter team now,’ he says. ‘It was like one-size-fits-all in my day. It was a physical encounter, we played the way England did and if someone goes down cheaply, you’re shouting at them to get up. That era has gone.

‘I remember when I was Under-21 coach, watching an Under-17 game between England and Spain. During the first half the Spanish central defender was kicking lumps out of our centre-forward.

‘When our player retaliated, the Spanish player rolled around on the floor and got our player booked. In other words, he fought tough but played clever and we have to adopt some of that. You can’t be so naïve that you lose your rag and kick someone. The Spanish defender caused the problem but our player picked up the tab for it.

‘We’ve become a lot more streetwise in English football, and in some ways that’s a shame. We watch players going down cheaply in the Premier League and it doesn’t sit well with the crowd. You can hear the complaining.

‘We have to take the good things about English football, like the tempo, but also incorporate one or two bits that will make us very effective on the international stage. We are doing a lot of things right. Since the national football centre was built at St George’s Park in 2012, we’ve had success at all levels, especially going to the latter stages of competitions.

‘There is a brilliant building process in place and we shouldn’t lose sight of that, but we just need to get our hands on a trophy at men’s senior level.’

'There is a brilliant building process in place and we shouldn’t lose sight of that, but we just need to get our hands on a trophy at men’s senior level,' says Pearce

'Gazza always had the arrogance on the pitch,’ Pearce recalls. ‘Even though he was a young kid, it was "Give me the ball, I’ll show you"'

While Thomas Tuchel’s team are among the favourites this summer, there were few such expectations when England travelled to Italy 36 years ago. English clubs were still banned from European competition following the Heysel Stadium tragedy in 1985, and police kept England fans under the tightest security, especially during the early stages of the tournament.

Robson was in the spotlight, too, having agreed to join PSV Eindhoven after the finals. There appeared little prospect of his team giving their fans anything to remember. What followed would change English football for good, and Pearce made an outstanding contribution to England’s march to the last four. Widely derided when they left for Italy, the players returned as heroes – with Gascoigne suddenly a national icon.

‘Gazza always had the arrogance on the pitch,’ Pearce recalls. ‘Even though he was a young kid, it was "Give me the ball, I’ll show you." No matter who he was playing against, his mentality was "‘I’ll show you I’m the best on the pitch."

‘A few England players like David Platt and Des Walker put their credentials on the table in that World Cup but Gazza was incredible from the moment he got into the side and Bobby Robson trusted him. Top players need a top stage and that was his.

‘That tournament had a lot of magic. At the time, Italy had the greatest league in the world – you had the AC Milan team, Diego Maradona was playing there, then Cameroon beat Argentina in the first game and a very good West German side lifted the trophy.

‘So many good things came from it and I see it as a forerunner to the Premier League. A lot of people who weren’t really football fans were converted and realised it was a brilliant game.

'All of a sudden musicians found it quite sexy to be involved and support a team whereas prior to Italia '90 people only seemed to talk about crowd trouble. It really was a turning point.’

Maradona is fouled by Guido Buchwald (left) and Lothar Mattheus of West Germany during the 1990 World Cup final in Rome

'The penalty miss taught me I had resilience. I couldn’t wait to get started again for Nottingham Forest the following season and it was one of the best of my career'

Pearce has long since been able to see past his penalty miss in Turin and still remembers the dignity of his opponents. ‘That night taught me a lot about humility in victory,’ he reflects. ‘I was one of the players selected for the random drugs test after the game.

‘Two German players, I don’t recall who, sat there with me in total silence for the best part of two hours, waiting to give a sample. They had just won a World Cup semi-final and I’d lost one. That was humility.

‘It taught me I had resilience. I couldn’t wait to get started again for Nottingham Forest the following season and it was one of the best of my career. I scored 16 goals from left-back, with no penalties.’

Pearce sees similar resolve in England’s vice-captain Declan Rice – and he should know. Pearce was part of David Moyes’ coaching staff during two spells at West Ham and helped the midfielder develop from promising talent into a player sold to Arsenal for £105million three years ago. Now he is a Premier League champion.

Yet heading into the tournament, some doubts remain about Rice. Fine player, yes. But on the same level as the world’s best in his position, like Pedri, Vitinha or Fede Valverde? The jury is still out on that one.

Former players have urged Rice to show he can bend a game to his will, with former Manchester United captain Roy Keane even suggesting the 27-year-old is ‘too nice’. ‘It’s the biggest compliment you could pay him,’ Pearce counters.

‘The top players are nice to a certain degree but on the pitch they have a steely determination to get where they want to go. I’ve been in dressing rooms after he’s made mistakes and he’s reacted very positively.

‘With Dec, you think he could win a game on his own, because of his physical prowess, his ability on the ball, and you’re thinking: "Maybe [he could do] a little bit more." I probably thought the same, back in the day at West Ham, but you don’t say that about many players.

‘I was renowned for taking free-kicks and I saw Dec score two wonder free-kicks against Real Madrid (in April 2025). I’ve barely seen him take one since. Like Dec, I could score from free-kicks and if I were him I’d be saying to my team-mates "Get out of my way. I’m taking this and I’m taking all of them, unless you can do better than me."’

'I saw Declan Rice score two wonder free-kicks against Real Madrid (in April 2025). I’ve barely seen him take one since,' says Pearce

'I've been involved in this Trident Community Foundation for six years,’ Pearce says. ‘The mental and physical health (benefits) are unbelievable'

Pearce’s anecdotes could run for days. He recollects how a Cameroon defender ‘just punched Gary Lineker on the halfway line’ during England’s stormy quarter-final win in 1990. He still regards Terry Venables’ team that reached the semi-finals of Euro 96 as the best England side he can remember (Pearce was only four when England won the World Cup in 1966).

Yet Pearce is here for another reason: the ‘fitness and football’ sessions that have helped numerous men with their mental health. Pearce did not take the gilded route through academy football – ‘I was an electrician and then three-and-a-half years later I’m stepping out at a World Cup’ – and understands how the game reaches the roots of every community.

‘I have been involved in this scheme for the best part of six years,’ Pearce says. ‘The mental and physical health aspects are unbelievable in terms of being part of a team and bringing people into the community.

‘I’ve visited a lot of clubs and met a number of the volunteers, as well as the people who’ve taken part. You see the uplift. Sometimes people are a bit lonely, or they want to get fitter, and the football club ends up being the hub. We see the top end of the game, the Premier League, but football starts here.’

The Trident Community Foundation, established by Entain's award-winning Pitching In programme, has awarded over £700,000 in grants to support projects at Trident League clubs across the country. Find out more at https://www.entaingroup.com/sustainability-esg/social-impact/pitching-in

Stuart was at Isthmian League side Grays Athletic in Thurrock visiting a fitness and football session which has helped men with their physical and mental health via a Pitching In Trident Community Fund Grant. https://www.isthmian.co.uk/articles/grant-helps-grays-locals-to-be-more-athletic

Sports.title: Ben Stokes DROPPED as Joe Root is named interim England Test captain in his absence - after all-rounder and Gus Atkinson were suspended following nightclub incident with 125kg Saracens rugby star
Sports.content:
Ben Stokes has been omitted from England’s second Test squad against New Zealand with Joe Root taking over as interim captain.

Stokes, 35, and Surrey seamer Gus Atkinson will not feature, the England and Wales Cricket Board said, while the investigation into their breaking of team protocols in the early hours of Monday morning is ongoing.

Harry Brook is the Test team’s vice-captain, and leads England in white-ball cricket, but the ECB have announced Stokes’ predecessor Joe Root as stand-in for the match at The Oval from next Wednesday.

Sussex fast bowler Jofra Archer and uncapped Essex batsman Jordan Cox have effectively replaced the two overlooked players in the 15-man squad.

England won the first Test at Lord’s by 115 runs, but that was overshadowed when it was revealed that Stokes and Atkinson had failed to adhere to a midnight curfew.

The pair were then caught up in an incident at a Chelsea nightclub in which a Saracens academy player Totoa Auvaa is alleged to have struck a member of the England team’s security staff.

Joe Root has been named as interim England Test captain in the absence of Ben Stokes

Stokes' international future is in doubt after he was caught up in a nightclub melee on Monday

It was anticipated that Brook, 27, would lead the team once doubts were cast on Stokes’ availability.

Yet in Brook’s Yorkshire team-mate Root, the ECB have chosen an older head and steady pair of hands.

Root, 35, led England in a record 64 Test matches between 2017-2022, but relinquished the post after one win in 17, and gave his blessing to close friend Stokes to succeed him.

In a statement released on Wednesday afternoon, the ECB said: 'The England & Wales Cricket Board can confirm that, given the ongoing investigation, Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson have not been made available for selection for the Rothesay second Test against New Zealand, which starts at the Kia Oval on Wednesday 17 June.

'Yorkshire batter Joe Root will lead the team as Interim Captain.

'Sussex fast bowler Jofra Archer and Essex batter Jordan Cox have been added to the squad.'

Daily Mail Sport reported on Tuesday that Stokes is understood to be considering his future as an England cricketer after he and Atkinson broke the team’s midnight curfew.

With the ECB’s investigation ongoing into the events at the Rex Rooms nightclub in Chelsea, Stokes has been at home in the North East weighing up his options.

Earlier on Sunday evening, Stokes was downing £25 double rum and cokes with England rugby captain Maro Itoje at a West London pub, before he was later caught up in the late night melee with another rugby player.

It was understood to have been sparked by a disagreement over tables in a VIP area of the club.

England squad for the second Test vs New Zealand Joe Root (Yorkshire) - Captain Rehan Ahmed (Leicestershire) Jofra Archer (Sussex) Sonny Baker (Hampshire) Shoaib Bashir (Derbyshire) Jacob Bethell (Warwickshire) Harry Brook (Yorkshire) Jordan Cox (Essex) Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire) Matthew Fisher (Surrey) Emilio Gay (Durham) James Rew (Somerset) Ollie Robinson (Sussex) Jamie Smith (Surrey) Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire)

One source close to the dressing room described questions surrounding his future as ‘up in the air’, after the ECB offered him time to think about his options. Another told Daily Mail Sport: ‘I don’t know if even he knows yet what he wants to do.’

The mood at Lord’s remains unwavering after the latest drink-related incident to dominate English cricket’s headlines – not least because Stokes himself was one of the architects, along with head coach Brendon McCullum and managing director Rob Key, of the curfew imposed after the disastrous tour of Australia. There is angry talk at HQ of the captain bringing the game into disrepute.

A statement on Monday evening from the governing body had said: 'The ECB is currently investigating a breach of team protocols following the conclusion of the first men's Test against New Zealand.

'Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were present at a nightclub in the early hours of Monday morning when an incident took place.

'We are currently seeking further information, and an announcement regarding the squad for the second Test will be made in due course.

'The Cricket Regulator has been informed and we will provide a further update when possible.'

Sports.title: West Ham sponsors did NOT know about safeguarding ban on David Sullivan - after he was blocked from having contact with club's women's and academy teams
Sports.content:
West Ham United's principal sponsor was not made aware of the safeguarding ban in place on the club's co-owner David Sullivan when it penned a multi-year deal, Daily Mail Sport understands.

Bosses at Boyle Sports, a major bookmaker who are free to remain on the front of shirt following the club's relegation from the Premier League, have been left 'extremely concerned' at accusations the 77-year-old preyed on young women for sex.

Sullivan, it emerged, has been forbidden from having contact with the club's women's and academy teams since 2023 due to safeguarding concerns following an FA investigation after officials were made aware of historical allegations against him.

The FA investigation is understood to remain active. Sullivan denies any wrongdoing.

Earlier this week Daily Mail Sport reported how the independent football regulator, which has the power to force owners to sell stakes should they not comply with its owners and directors test, had requested urgent information from West Ham on the matter.

West Ham's principal sponsor was not made aware of the safeguarding ban in place on the club's co-owner David Sullivan when it penned a multi-year deal, Daily Mail Sport understands

Boyle Sports signed a multi-year deal in 2025. The terms are not known but the deal is worth multiple millions.

Had the Hammers stayed in the top flight they would not have been able to remain on the front of shirt thanks to new rules.

A Boyle Sports spokesperson said: 'Boyle Sports is extremely concerned at the serious nature of the allegations levelled against David Sullivan.

'It is our understanding that the Independent Football Regulator is reviewing this matter urgently and we wholeheartedly support their efforts in doing so.'

In a new statement, Sullivan said he had negotiated a temporary agreement with the FA not to meet academy or women's team players '1-2-1' until a historical anonymous complaint was resolved. He has previously said he denies allegations of wrongdoing.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi and Argentina team-mates have passport details LEAKED in bizarre team sheet data breach
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi and Argentina team-mates have passport details LEAKED in bizarre team sheet data breach

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Lionel Messi and his Argentina team-mates were involved in a bizarre data breach before a pre-World Cup friendly that saw their passport details accidentally leaked.

Lionel Scaloni's side beat Iceland 3-0 in Alabama in the early hours of Wednesday morning (GMT) in front of 88,000 fans.

When countries submit team sheets ahead of kick off, these sometimes include passport numbers of their players, although that private information is normally blurred out or deleted before being shared to the media.

However, Argentina's team sheet - which included Messi, Chelsea star Enzo Fernandez and Man United's Lisandro Martinez - was released with their passport numbers still on there, and this was reproduced by several local media outlets.

This damaging security leak therefore exposed the details for the entire Argentina starting XI and substitutes.

The error appeared to be the responsibility of Road to '26, the Turkish Airlines-sponsored company who were in charge of organising the friendly. They have arranged multiple other pre-tournament games in the USA too.

Lionel Messi and his Argentina team-mates were involved in a bizarre data breach before a pre-World Cup friendly that saw their passport details accidentally leaked

Iceland didn't include the passport numbers of their players on their team sheet, so they managed to avoid a similar leak.

During the match, Messi scored a penalty shortly after coming off the bench in the 70th minute.

Valentin Barco earlier put Scaloni's side ahead in the first half, before Thiago Almada then made it 3-0 late on.

Speaking after the game, Messi - who had picked up a hamstring injury last month when playing for Inter Miami - provided an update on his own fitness and hopes for Argentina this summer.

'I’m happy, enjoying every moment, and excited as always,' he said. 'I felt really good.

'I wanted to get going and shake off the lingering fears that come with an injury - to be able to play freely.

'We have a week left to get everyone in top shape and be ready for the opener.'

Messi played a huge role in Argentina's World Cup triumph in 2022 and they have also won the last two Copa America titles.

This time around the reigning champions face Algeria, Jordan and Austria in their group, with their first game coming next Wednesday against the North African side.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi's Argentina swansong and Cristiano Ronaldo gunning for glory with Portugal: The football superstars who will see out their last dance at the 2026 World Cup
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi's Argentina swansong and Cristiano Ronaldo gunning for glory with Portugal: The football superstars who will see out their last dance at the 2026 World Cup

Consider yourself a World Cup expert? Challenge yourself with our exclusive quiz for free by signing up to our World Cup newsletter. Get it HERE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The 2026 World Cup is on the horizon, with the opening game set to take place on Thursday as Mexico welcome South Africa in the opener of the 23rd edition of football's greatest tournament.

The stage is set and for many young players it is a chance to shine. However, this year's global tournament will also serve as a curtain call for some of football's biggest stars.

Among those set to play at their last World Cup finals this summer are Premier League greats, titans of the international game, and even former World Cup winners.

Here, Daily Mail Sport waves farewell to some of the greatest players to play the game in their last dance at international level.

Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal)

Number of World Cups played: 5

First World Cup appearance: Angola vs Portugal, June 11 2006

A hero for many football lovers across the planet, Cristiano Ronaldo will play in his sixth World Cup boasting an impressive record alongside Guillermo Ochoa and Lionel Messi as the only players to have featured in six or more World Cups.

Cristiano Ronaldo will be looking to go out on a high at this summer's World Cup in America

The 41-year-old made his debut at the finals a staggering 20 years ago and has been a fixture in the side at every tournament since

The Portuguese phenomenon has notched eight goals and provided two assists in 22 appearances in this tournament and became the first and only player in history to score in five different World Cup campaigns in Qatar 2022.

Dubbed by international teammate Bruno Fernandes as, 'the best striker in the world, and the greatest player in football history,' it is clear for all to see the lasting impact Ronaldo has left at both international and club level. Yet still, many critics highlight the 41-year-old's ego as a threat to his nation's chances of going far in the tournament.

Despite the outside noise, Ronaldo will yet again lead his country in their opening game a week from now against the Democratic Republic of Congo who feature in their first tournament since 1974.

If Portugal are to have a say in the outcome of the 2026 World Cup, make no mistake that Ronaldo will have something to do with it. A grandstand finish looks on the cards for Portugal's main man.

Lionel Messi (Argentina)

Number of World Cups played: 5

First World Cup appearance: Argentina vs Serbia and Montenegro, June 16 2006

After the incredible finish to the 2022 World Cup final in Qatar between Argentina and France, Lionel Messi finally got his hands on the trophy he had been chasing his whole career.

He teased the idea of retiring from international football before the campaign in 2022 saying, 'It's my last World Cup surely.' Four years later and the Argentine magician has remained in Lionel Scaloni's 26-man squad as they aim to become the first nation since 1962 to defend a World Cup title.

Lionel Messi achieved immortality in Argentina when he captained his side to their third World Cup victory in 2022

But there has been an injury scare for Messi ahead of this summer's tournament, with the 38-year-old having to be replaced in the 73rd minute of Inter Miami's 6-4 victory against Philadelphia Union just over two weeks ago. He was rested in Argentina's penultimate international friendly on the weekend against Honduras.

Messi holds the all-time leading appearance record in World Cups with 26. He has scored 13 goals and provided eight assists in these appearances and in Qatar he was involved in ten of his nation's 15 goals – a campaign that cemented him, as he has been so often throughout his career, as the man for the big occasion.

Argentina kickstart their tournament against Algeria in Kansas City next Wednesday. It is unclear yet whether Messi will feature against the Algerians, but one thing is for sure whether his minutes are limited or not: the superstar from Rosario has given generations of Argentinians hope that their country will win the World Cup for a fourth time.

Neymar Jr (Brazil)

Number of World Cups played: 3

First World Cup appearance: Brazil vs Croatia, June 12 2014

A man once affectionately labelled 'O Menino de Ouro' (the golden boy) by his boyhood club Santos has come a long way from the hardships he faced growing up in Sao Paolo.

Neymar has had an illustrious career and is celebrated as an icon across Brazil by fans - and even his international teammates - which is no surprise as to why his inclusion in the 2026 Brazil squad by Carlo Ancelotti was such a massive boost for his country.

For Brazilians, the name Neymar means more than just football. Neymar is a symbol of joy, creativity, flair and audacity and has made so many fall in love with watching him play. But the 34-year-old veteran has faced similar injury concerns as former Barcelona teammate Lionel Messi, with a calf problem keeping him out for the time being.

Neymar experienced his maiden World Cup on home soil in 2014 after missing out on selection four years earlier

An injury-troubled veteran Carlo Ancelotti hopes that the star will be a talismanic presence for the squad this summer

Whilst he may be sidelined for a portion of Brazil's group stage fixtures, his inclusion in the Selecao's 26-man squad sparked mini celebrations across the nation.

The all-time leading scorer for Brazil is not shy of putting on a performance and has grabbed headlines in previous tournaments ranging from his outrageous skills to his even more outrageous haircuts.

With injuries causing a stop-start season with Santos, all signs point to this being Neymar's last World Cup. Brazil will be hoping to give their man a perfect send off, winning the World Cup for the first time since 2002 in an attempt to repay their golden boy for everything he has given to them.

Luka Modric (Croatia)

Number of World Cups played: 4

First World Cup appearance: Japan vs Croatia, June 18 2006

Renowned for his elegant style of play and press resistance on the grandest of stages, few players embody the phrase 'aged like a fine wine' as Luka Modric does. Now playing his football in Italy for AC Milan the Croatian midfielder has typified what it means to be a true professional.

Modric scored what was perhaps his final goal on Croatian soil on Saturday in an international friendly against Slovenia. At 40 years old he is still the heartbeat of Croatia's side, and adored by many fans across the globe. Nicknamed 'The Maestro' he will feature in fifth World Cup this summer as Croatia take on England in their opening game.

Throughout his career, Modric has always been a very intelligent footballer, and this has allowed him to outclass his opposition, even when his legs get heavy, through timing and decision making. With 196 caps, no one has represented Croatia more than Modric has. His longevity and hunger to play is a true credit to who he is as an athlete and person.

Luka Modric has been a mainstay in the Croatian set-up and continues as one of their key stars

Modric will captain a side looking to hit the heights they hit in 2018, when they reached the World Cup final for the first time in their nation's history despite being beaten 4-1 by France. It looks unlikely that Modric will take part in another World Cup, and for football fans everywhere his name will live long in the memory for what he has achieved throughout his sparkling career.

Manuel Neuer (Germany)

Number of World Cups played: 4

First World Cup appearance: Germany vs Australia, June 14 2010

Julian Nagelsmann announced ahead of the 2026 World Cup that 40-year-old Manuel Neuer will be the first-choice keeper for Germany. Neuer has redefined what it means to be a goalkeeper in the modern day, often recognised for his ability to play out the back with his feet and act as another defender earning himself the nickname 'The Sweeper Keeper'.

Throughout his incredible career, Neuer has won 33 major professional trophies including 13 Bundesliga trophies, two UEFA Champions League trophies and - of course - the 2014 World Cup as Germany beat Argentina 1-0 thanks to a Mario Goetze goal deep into extra time. He also won the Golden Glove award in 2014 with four clean sheets in seven appearances.

After Germany's quarter-final defeat in the 2024 Euros to tournament winners Spain, Neuer announced that he would be retiring from international football. Now ahead of this summer's tournament, Nagelsmann intends to go all the way and has named the 'aura and quality' that Neuer brings to team as a big part of his optimism.

Manuel Neuer is one of only a handful of players at this World Cup featuring over the age of 40

Germany, as always, are strong contenders for the 2026 World Cup trophy and just like their success 12 years ago in Brazil, Neuer remains a huge part of the way the Germans build up their football from back to front as well as being an incredible shot-stopper.

His eventual retirement from international football will be a huge miss as he is widely regarded as one of the greatest goalkeepers to have ever played the game.

Mohamed Salah (Egypt)

Number of World Cups played: 1

First World Cup appearance: Russia vs Egypt, June 19 2018

The Egyptian King, Mohamed Salah, will play in his second World Cup tournament after making his debut back in 2018 in Russia. After a turbulent season at club level with Liverpool, Salah will be hoping to end his season on a high with the fifth-highest-ranking African side in the competition.

Salah will captain the Pharaohs against Belgium in their first game of the 2026 World Cup and has stated, 'we want to make people proud of us, and we will do our utmost.' The two-times African Player of the Year is aiming for his side to go further than any Egyptian team has gone in the tournament.

Turning 34 in a week's time, Salah has unfinished business on the world stage. He scored twice in his nation's campaign in Russia eight years ago but is still yet to taste a victory in the competition. He has been on the losing side twice in both 2017 and 2021 during the African Cup of Nations, but former captain Ahmed Fathi has backed him to 'achieve something with the Pharaohs at the 2026 World Cup'.

Despite having enjoying a heavily decorated playing career with Liverpool, Mohamed Salah has only featured at one World Cup

'He always made the difference, and I hope he will do it again in the United States', Fathi told AFP.

With his move away from Liverpool at the end of this season, there is no denying that this is likely to be Salah's last involvement in a World Cup. The king of Egypt has brought joy to so many of his admirers throughout his decorated career and is a beacon of pride for many Africans.

James Rodriguez (Colombia)

Number of World Cups played: 3

First World Cup appearance: Colombia vs Greece, June 14 2014

When we talk about the World Cup, it is hard to forget the delicious strike a 22-year-old James Rodriguez scored in Brazil in 2014 in the round of 16 against Uruguay. Brazuca plucked out of the air, controlled on his chest, left-footed volley, crossbar and in. A goal to take your breath away and Rodriguez will always be a part of international folklore because of the magic he provided that night in Rio.

His inclusion in Colombia's 2026 World Cup squad marks his third global tournament and is considered by many as his last. The 34-year-old departed MLS side Minnesota United so he could focus solely on his preparations for the 2026 World Cup.

Rodriguez, together with Bayern Munich's Luis Diaz, contributed to 17 of Colombia's 28 goals in World Cup qualifying. He comes alive when playing for Colombia and was named player of the tournament in their 2024 Copa America campaign despite losing by one goal to nil against Argentina in the final.

James Rodriguez burst into international consciousness with his stunning appearance at the World Cup in Brazil 12 years ago

Despite facing many injury problems throughout his career, the Colombian is often viewed as the face of his nation's football team. Sitting just four assists off Carlos Valderrama's record, there is no doubt the midfielder will be keen to etch his name into Colombian football history in what will be his final act on the World stage.

Riyad Mahrez (Algeria)

Number of World Cups played: 1

First World Cup appearance: Belgium vs Algeria, June 17 2014

If you cast your mind back to the 2015-16 Premier League season, Riyad Mahrez is a man who knows the true meaning of defying the odds. An inspiration for many Algerians, Mahrez has remained elegant and dangerous despite his increasing age.

After failing to qualify for the 2018 and 2022 World Cup campaigns, Algeria come into this tournament as Africa's fourth highest rank side. Mahrez will captain his nation as they take on the holders Argentina in their first game. The 35-year-old is undoubtedly the one to watch for his country who have strong ambitions of progressing to the knockout round of the competition.

Riyad Mahrez has scarcely played World Cup football but will enjoy his swansong with Algeria on the biggest stage this summer

He has already made the statement that this World Cup will be his last and in an open training session at the Nelson-Mandela stadium in Baraki, Mahrez and his international teammates saluted the Algerian supporters for the last time before they travelled to North America.

Contributing to 75 goals in 113 appearances, the Al-Ahli winger has been a true servant to his nation. Mahrez will be hoping to leave his mark at this tournament, guiding his team into the knockout stages as they did in 2014 where they were unpicked by Germany. Mahrez has changed the way football is played in Algeria and will undoubtedly go down as one of the most talented African players of all time.

Sports.title: World Class Bike Racing comes to London this weekend in new major cycling event
Sports.content:
World Class Bike Racing comes to London this weekend in new major cycling event

The City of London Nocturne returns this weekend, transforming the Square Mile into a high-speed cycling circuit across two days of racing and festival entertainment. From charity team relays featuring pro riders and corporate teams on Friday to elite criterium races on Saturday, the event will showcase a packed programme of cycling action, world-record attempts, and community races, all set against the backdrop of the City’s iconic streets.

View Image The City of London Nocturne will bring a festival of racing to the Square Mile this weekend. On Friday 12th and Saturday 13th June

The City of London Nocturne will bring a festival of racing to the Square Mile this weekend. On Friday 12th and Saturday 13th June, two wheels will be at the heart of the City, kicking off with the GOSH City Criterium on Friday. This new charity Pro-Am team challenge will see 20 corporate teams joined by pro riders on a closed road circuit around Guildhall in a team relay format.

‌



The cohort of pros taking part is a mixture of current elite cyclists and some legends of the sport, notably triple Olympic champion, Ed Clancy, and Giro d’Italia stage winner, Alex Dowsett.

‌



They will be raising money for the new Children Cancer Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital. Then on Saturday, the action continues with racing taking place on a thrilling 1.3 km closed-road circuit weaving through Cheapside and Bank, right in the heart of the City of London.

‌



The racing programme runs from midday to 10pm with a host of exciting events including:

The Brompton Folding Bike Race

The Voi Bike Challenge - a cycle hire race where riders must ride responsibly to avoid penalties!

The Limitless Race supported by Shell UK - a multi discipline para cycling race

Guinness World Records title attempts featuring the world’s largest Penny Farthing

Rugby star nominated for global award after FOUR YEARS without touching a ball READ MORE :

The action concludes with the men’s and women’s elite races, bringing a star-studded criterium line-up to the City streets. The women’s field features British Criterium Champion, Kate Richardson as well as GB Cycling Team members Megan Barker (Rapha Cycling Club), Sophie Lewis (DAS Hutchinson), and Josie Knight (DAS Hutchinson).

‌



And in the men’s field, British Criterium Champion, Cameron Mason (Alpecin Premier-Tech), Canadian Criterium Champion, Mathias Guillemette (Tudor Pro Cycling), former Lidl –Trek and UAE-Emirates pro, Ryan Gibbons, Olympic silver medallist, Ollie Wood (Rapha Cycling Club) and former British Criterium Champion, Matt Bostock (Rapha Cycling Club) will all compete.

There will be festival atmosphere around the racing including the Cheapside Business Alliance Fan Zone at the Royal Exchange which will have a big screen providing a live feed of the racing.

This event is supported by the City of London, the City of London Destination City Fund, and the Cheapside Business Alliance. It is free to attend for spectators, while the elite races will be broadcast live on TNT Sports and HBO max from 8pm on Saturday.

‌



For a full event schedule go to www.racenocturne.com

ABOUT CITY OF NOCTURNE

Nocturne is a night-time criterium (circuit race). In partnership with the City of London, we are bringing world-class cycle racing to the City streets on 12-13 June 2026. The reimagined Nocturne will span two action-packed days, introducing an exciting new format designed to create a spectacular festival of bike racing.
